prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which trapped atoms at the magic wavelength to reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and opened new regimes of precision measurement

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a new measurement capability rather than an incremental improvement. Katori's magic-wavelength idea makes the light shift of the clock transition cancel, so thousands of atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime with no Doppler or recoil shift, and the statistical power of an ensemble is combined with the systematic control of a single trapped particle. Ye's group then took strontium to the 1e-18 level, and clocks now resolve gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences, constrain drifts of fundamental constants and are the leading route to a redefinition of the SI second. The experimental evidence is what I look for: many independent laboratories (Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, and others) have reproduced the performance on Sr, Yb and other species, and international clock comparisons confirm the uncertainty budgets. The two-name credit is unusually clean. This is progress limited by how precisely we can measure, and a field-opening instrument with uses (geodesy, dark-matter searches, networks of clocks) that are only starting to appear.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes. The 2005 prize covered frequency combs, including Hall's work, which made optical clocks countable, and the 2012 prize covered trapped-ion control and ion clocks. A skeptical colleague can call the lattice clock a second-generation refinement of already-honoured technology. There is also the timing argument that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the full consequence is still prospective. Finally, the credit has edges: the Sr, Yb and Hg lattice-clock groups and the ion-clock groups (NIST Al+, for instance) are not all covered by two names, and I cannot settle from the supplied list how much of the 1e-18 milestone belongs to the Ye group versus its collaborators.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B018 first, calls the Katori and Ye credit unusually clear, and considers the recognition timely and arguably overdue relative to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
responses.response: I agree on the clarity of credit, and I share her view that we should not treat the 2005 and 2012 prizes as having already covered this. The frequency comb is the ruler that reads out an optical clock, and the 2012 prize was for control of a single quantum system. Neither includes the central trick here, which is engineering a lattice in which the clock transition is unperturbed while an ensemble is interrogated. Where I would qualify her view: both of us come from the atomic-physics side, so we may be underweighting how the other members see the overlap. I would want the citation to say lattice clock and magic wavelength explicitly so the distinction from the earlier prizes is on the page.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B007) first as a new observational window opened by a very large instrument, and he lists B018 second while asking whether it is a distinct discovery or an extension of the frequency-comb prize.
responses.response: I take the instrument argument seriously, since I weigh new instruments heavily myself, and I accept that the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux is confirmed in several channels. My difficulty is attribution: Pearce himself notes that a discovery by several hundred collaborators is hard to assign to two or three people and that Yoshida's role is less decisive, so the configuration he proposes (Halzen and Karle) leaves out a large part of the credit. Source identification beyond TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 is at evidence level rather than discovery level. On his comb question: a comb alone does not make a lattice clock. Katori's proposal and the JILA strontium work depend on the lattice physics and cavity-stabilised lasers, which are a distinct contribution. I would rank B007 high on science but lower on the readiness of the credit.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B008) first as the architecture of essentially all superconducting quantum processors, and notes that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits left light-matter coupling unrecognised.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is a major, thoroughly reproduced advance, and the 2004 theory and experiment pairing is well documented. My qualification is about internal competition inside the supplied credit: Girvin, whom Johansson himself calls a painful omission, would be left out of any three-person split, and the prize would come soon after the 2025 award for the same device platform. I also note that he flags his own proximity to the field. I rank B008 below the lattice clock mainly because of this credit and timing problem, not because of its science, and I keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Olsson ranks room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance (B003) first for its clear observable, documented societal benefit and full maturity, and puts B018 third.
responses.response: The 1995 results of Miyazaki and Moodera are a clean experimental discovery, and I agree that read-head impact is concrete. I would ask, however, how much of the later device success depends on the MgO-barrier advances she herself assigns to Parkin as the second wave. If that is where the large magnetoresistance came from, a prize for the 1995 work alone rewards the opening step while the decisive reliability came later, and the credit then becomes a real dispute. For the lattice clock the opening idea and the decisive demonstrations sit with the same two groups, so the attribution question is easier to settle.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to wait for the SI second redefinition before recognising lattice clocks, or regards the 1e-18 results and geodesy tests as already sufficient impact.
How members who see B018 as an extension of the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes weigh the distinct role of the magic-wavelength lattice.
Whether other early lattice-clock groups (Yb, Hg) or the ion-clock groups have credit claims that two names cannot cover.
statement.conflict_note: Possible connection: Jun Ye is at JILA and worked closely with John Hall, in whose Boulder laboratory I spent a year during my PhD, so there is a personal-scientific link to the Hall-Ye environment, though I have no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye that is apparent from my profile. For the alternatives, B023 (solid-state spins) lies close to my own rare-earth-crystal quantum-information work, and B008 involves the Chalmers-led WACQT environment where I am on the management team together with fellow member Goran Johansson. I would consider recusal on those candidates, but no specific conflict on B018 is apparent from the provided profile.
